newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank to plan for EMU in M3 strategy talks. [CORRECTED 18:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank to plan for EMU in M3 strategy talks. [CORRECTED 18:55 GMT]

text.p: When the German central bank meets this week to set its traditional money supply growth target it will have to accept that, if all goes as planned in Europe, its monetary policy days are almost over.

The Bundesbank traditionally sets a one-year target for growth in M3 money supply in the following year just before its Christmas break. It argues that M3 is the best guide to future inflation in the economy and so to interest rate policy needs.
But this year, Europe's most powerful central bank will be all too aware that time is running out until it hands over the reins of monetary policy to the European Central Bank in 1999.
The bank's chief economist Otmar Issing has already said that the Bundesbank will look ahead to the transfer of monetary policy power to the ECB when it sets its target this Thursday.
Analysts were united in the view that there would be no major policy shift away from monetary targeting -- even though the Bundesbank will almost certainly miss its goal in 1996.
But they were divided on exactly how the goal would look.
Some said the Bundesbank may take the bull by the horns and set a two-year target to cover 1997 and 1998, even though it has often shunned a longer-term target in the past.
"From a strategic point of view this may be acceptable if it limits market volatility due to inevitable M3 swings in the run-up to EMU," Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt said.

Yet a thin majority in a Reuter poll of 16 financial institutes said it was unlikely the central bank would shift entirely away from the pattern seen over the last 20 years, and would again set a one-year expansion target.

The Bundesbank's council could nonetheless pave the way for a difficult transition year in 1998 -- when the ECB will be appointing policy-makers and assembling its monetary armour -- by giving an extra, longterm money supply guideline, some said.

"At the end of 1997, only a few months before the decision on which countries will participate in European monetary union, it could prove to be advantageous for the Bundesbank to have already fixed the trend of its 1998 money supply policy," said Hermann Remsperger, chief economist at BHF-Bank.

"The Bundesbank is certainly aware of the institutional gap in monetary policy which will open up in 1998," he added. "The decision on participating nations means monetary union begins de facto before 1999, without a monetary policy institute."
Remsperger, in common with nine other economists out of a total of 18 polled, believed the Bundesbank would stick with a one-year target this year.
But he predicted that the central bank would also indicate an average growth path for M3 in both 1997 and 1998, so providing orientation for its policy in 1998 long in advance.
WestLB chief economist Ulrich Hombrecher and economists at Dresdner Bank also argued in favour of a one-year goal.
"In our estimation the Bundesbank is unlikely to alter its method for deducing the target range just two years before the switch-over to EMU," Dresdner Bank said in a commentary.

The Bundesbank traditionally compiles its M3 target by looking at likely developments in growth and prices, making adjustments for changes in the way in which money is being used, and then placing a target corridor around its central estimate of M3 growth needs.

For 1996, it set a corridor of four to six percent, based on an assessment of production potential at 2.5 percent, unavoidable inflation of two percent and a one percent element to compensate for slower velocity of circulation of money.
Velocity of circulation is a measure of how intensively funds are used in the economy.
Regardless of whether a two-year or one-year target is set this year, economists expect the methodology to be the same, and say the underlying assumptions will also be similar.

Among those economists polled, eight said they expected the target to be set on Thursday to be unchanged from 1996, and seven expected a slightly lower growth range. The other three gave only a central expansion rate not a target range.

Almost all of the economists polled expected the central bank to hold its leading interest rates steady at this week's meeting, with a minority (Corrects from majority) view predicting that the central bank would trim its three percent money market rate slightly.
